# Variations in how medical researchers report patient demographics: a retrospective analysis of published articles

**Authors:** Erika E Lynn-Green; Avery A Ofoje; Robert H Lynn-Green; David S Jones

**Affiliations:** aHarvard Medical School, 25 Shattuck Street, Boston, MA 02115, USA | bThe Medical University of South Carolina, 171 Ashley Avenue, Charleston, SC 29425, USA | cMathematica Inc., 1100 First St NE #1200, Washington, DC 20002, USA

## Abstract

The use of demographic variables in the medical literature has been a topic of much recent debate. Recent studies found that race and socioeconomic status (SES) are inconsistently reported. Best-practice use of sex and gender has been contentious. We aimed to characterise the state of medical demographic reporting in greater detail, especially regarding geography and specific terms used in articles.

Original articles were included from issues of the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM), JAMA, The Lancet, and the American Journal of Epidemiology (AJE) published from 1 January to 31 December 2020 (n = 640). Articles without human participants, case reports, or with only aggregate data were excluded, leaving 594 articles. Use of age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, and SES were coded, as well as corresponding author and participant geography.

99.0% of articles reported age. While 92.9% reported sex alone, only 4.7% used the term gender and 1.0% transgender. 47.8% of articles reported race and 29.6% reported ethnicity. Studies with U.S. corresponding authors or participants were significantly more likely to report race (72.9% and 73.7% respectively) or ethnicity (47.3% and 45.3% respectively) than those without (25.9% and 25.6% for race, 14.2% and 16.3% for ethnicity), p < 0.01 for all. Of articles reporting race, 40.9% used only a Black-white binary; of those reporting ethnicity, 85.2% included two or fewer terms. Under 5.0% of all articles used Office of Management and Budget (OMB) categories. Across all articles, 33.0% reported SES, from 15.2% in NEJM to 80.2% in AJE.

We found that while some factors (age, sex) are reported consistently, others (gender, race, ethnicity, SES) are not, despite recent attention. Authors often rely on binary or limited categories that inadequately capture human diversity. The presence of U.S. researchers or participants increased the reporting of race and/or ethnicity, highlighting wide variations that persist even as multinational collaborations become widespread. Researchers should reflect on their use of these terms, justify their decisions, and report results with care.

None.

Keywords: Medical literature, Diversity, Patient demographics

## Evidence before this study

We searched for “race,” “ethnicity,” and “socioeconomic status” with “demographics medical literature” on Google Scholar on 14 November 2020 and identified fourteen studies that showed that race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status (SES) were under- or inconsistently reported across medical journals, largely in specialty-specific literature. An additional literature search on 10 January 2023 revealed four papers published in the interim that found similar results in major medical journals.

## Added value of this study

To further clarify current practices and identify possible targets for reform, we examined in detail the descriptive statistics of a broader set of articles with greater attention to the specifics of demographic terms and how usage varied across researchers and participants in different countries, novel contributions to the literature. We based our study on an analysis of the two highest impact US medical journals, NEJM and JAMA, with high-impact comparisons also novel to the literature: a UK journal (The Lancet) to enable broader geographic comparisons and an epidemiology journal (AJE) to explore whether disciplinary standards differed.

## Implications of all the available evidence

The decisions that researchers make about what to report reflect their judgments about what really matters, and inform the judgments that others make, potentially with regrettable consequences. Researchers need to reflect on their use of sex, gender, race, ethnicity, and SES, to justify their decisions when they do so, and to report results with care.

## Introduction

All clinical research faces a basic question: can results derived from one group of people be applied to others? To help clinicians determine this, researchers report baseline characteristics of their study population, from age and sex to risk factors, comorbidities, and medical care. Efforts to characterise patients precisely and comprehensively have become increasingly important with growing interest in both personalised medicine and the social determinants of health.

Policies about best practices for the collection and reporting of demographic descriptors, which have been debated for decades, have become increasingly controversial. The 1993 U.S. NIH Revitalization Act, which sought to increase the inclusion of women and minoritised groups in clinical research, asked researchers to examine whether sex, gender, race, or ethnicity mattered in their analyses and, if so, to report data by these categories.1 U.S. researchers were advised to follow the categories defined by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB): five races (American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, or White) and two ethnicities (Hispanic or Latino, or not).2 The data standard for sex was simply male or female.2

Researchers continue to debate when and how such categories should be used, in medicine and in society more widely.3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 Is race a reflection of ancestry and genetics, a social construct, a product of racism, or all of those things? Do the OMB categories capture the complexity of human diversity and identity? Different countries parse diversity differently, with different expectations and requirements for researchers.11 This is increasingly relevant as international collaborations and multi-sited studies become widespread.

Recent evidence has found that race, ethnicity, and socioeconomic status (SES) are still under- or inconsistently reported across major journals.12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20 Labels for sex (referring to biological characteristics) and gender (referring to sociological characteristics) have also become contentious, with calls to standardise and clarify their use in academic settings as the rising visibility of sexual and gender minority patients has exposed the inadequacy of a male-female binary variable.21, 22, 23 Furthermore, researchers now recognize the profound impact of socioeconomic status (e.g., income, education, insurance status, etc.) and exposures (e.g., environmental, racism, structural violence, etc.) on health and treatment outcomes.24, 25, 26 Despite this, neither federal funders nor journal editors have defined best practices for the use or reporting of SES variables.27,28

To further clarify recent practices and identify possible targets for reform, we examined in detail the descriptive statistics used in articles in three top medical journals and one top epidemiology journal, paying particular attention to the specifics of what terms were used, and how. We also examined how usage varied across researchers and participants in different countries, a novel contribution to the literature. Many recent studies have focused on journals in a specific specialty. We chose instead to examine the most highly-read medical literature and analysed the two highest impact US medical journals, the New England Journal of Medicine (NEJM) and Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). We then pursued two high-impact comparisons: a UK journal (The Lancet) to enable broader geographic comparisons, and an epidemiology journal (the American Journal of Epidemiology, AJE) to explore whether and how disciplinary standards differed.

## Methods

### Search strategy and selection criteria

We undertook a retrospective analysis of published articles from 1 January to 31 December 2020 in NEJM, JAMA, Lancet, and AJE. We found 640 research reports but excluded articles that did not report data about individual humans (e.g., tissue sample analyses, modelling studies, statistical papers); case studies with fewer than five participants; and aggregate analyses (e.g., data reported at national levels without demographics) (Fig. 1; Supplemental Table S2). Meta-analyses were included if they reported data on patient demographics. This process yielded 594 original articles (Fig. 1; Table 1).

### Data analysis

We analysed what information each article included about age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, or SES. If this was not reported in a table, we searched the text for any occurrences of relevant terms (Supplemental Table S1). Each article was coded to indicate whether specific variables—age, sex, gender, race, ethnicity, SES—were reported (e.g., the variable was present or absent). If a variable was reported, we noted the specific language used. We also recorded the geographic locations of the corresponding authors and participants, as noted in the article or elsewhere (e.g., clinicaltrials.gov). Initial data collection and analysis was undertaken by E.E.L., A.A.O., and R.H.L. The coding of each article was then additionally checked by the senior author D.S.J., with all data therefore verified by two authors. We developed policies to address ambiguous cases and assign geographical authorship (Supplemental Appendix 1); these were resolved by the first author E.E.L.

We calculated the percentage of articles that reported each variable across all four journals and for each journal. We also calculated percentages according to geography based on whether the corresponding author (an imperfect proxy for where the research was centred) was in the U.S., and whether any of the research participants resided in the U.S. Chi-squared tests for geographical comparisons were performed by E.E.L. using R Studio, Version 1.2.5033.

Institutional review board approval was not required as no human participants were involved. No funding was obtained.

### Role of the funding source

There was no funding source for this study. All data were available to all authors, and all authors were responsible for the decision to submit this manuscript.

## Results

Nearly all articles (588, 99.0%) identified the age of the research participants, typically reporting the mean age in each group (Table 1, Fig. 2).

*Fig. 2: Proportions of articles from each journal that included information about the research participants' demographics.*

Nearly all articles (580, 97.6%) reported sex or gender (Table 1, Fig. 2). Most of those articles (552, 92.9%) reported sex alone, almost exclusively as male-female. Only 28 (4.7% of all articles) used “gender”; most of those (23 of 28) did not distinguish “gender” from “sex,” used “gender” in place of “sex,” or used it interchangeably with “sex” (Fig. 3a). Only 6 articles (1.0% of the total) used “transgender”; five of those articles focused explicitly on sexual and gender minority research participants or questions. We could not determine how the other 588 studies handled transgender participants.

*Fig. 3: a: Proportions of articles that used language about participants' sex alone, that mentioned gender, or that mentioned transgender participants. b: Proportions of articles that included language about either participants' race or ethnicity, that included language on both race and ethnicity, and that distinguished the terms race and ethnicity from each other as opposed to conflating them as one variable.*

Race was specified in 284 articles (47.8%) and ethnicity in 176 (29.6%) (Table 1). These are an overlapping set: 312 (52.5%) reported race or ethnicity, 157 (26.4%) reported both, 127 (21.4%) reported race alone, and only 19 (3.2%) reported ethnicity alone (Fig. 3b). Of the 157 that reported both, only 52 (33.1%) separated them as distinct categories (Fig. 3b). Specific language varied widely (Table 2). Of the 284 articles that reported race, 133 used two or fewer terms, usually a Black-white (or Black-non-Black) binary (116 articles, 40.9%). Of the 176 articles that reported ethnicity, 150 (85.2%) included two or fewer terms, usually Hispanic or not. Of the 312 articles that reported race or ethnicity, 204 (65.4%) also included an undefined “other” category. Only 18 articles (3.0%) used the exact language of the OMB categories, and only 24 articles (4.0%) mentioned the OMB categories in any form, including with some categories combined.

The use of categories for race or ethnicity varied significantly with geography (Fig. 4, Table 3). Assessing the geography of the publications was complex, because of the high prevalence of articles that listed both U.S. and non-U.S. authors (255, 42.9%) and the challenge of assessing the intellectual home of the project. Of the 594 articles, 277 (46.6%) had a U.S. corresponding author, and 274 (46.1%) included U.S. research participants (Table 1). Studies with a U.S. corresponding author were significantly more likely to report race (202, 72.9%) than those without a U.S. corresponding author (82 reported race, 25.9%) by chi-squared test (χ2 = 129, p < 0.01). Articles with any U.S. participants were also significantly more likely to report race (202, 73.7%) than articles without U.S. participants (82 reported race, 25.6%) (χ2 = 135, p < 0.01). Ethnicity data showed a similar pattern: for U.S. corresponding authors, 131 articles (47.3%) reported ethnicity, as opposed to 45 (14.2%) articles with non-U.S. corresponding authors (χ2 = 76, p < 0.01). One hundred and twenty-four (45.3%) articles with any U.S. participants reported ethnicity, while 52 (16.3%) without U.S. participants did so (χ2 = 58, p < 0.01).

Thirty-five unique countries were represented in the affiliations of corresponding authors, with country-level proportions reporting age, gender or sex, race or ethnicity, or SES presented in Table 3. Five corresponding authors reported two country affiliations; for the analyses in Table 3, their articles were categorised under both countries. Articles with U.S. corresponding authors were by far the most prevalent at 277, with the U.K. (70), Canada (42), China (25), and Australia (20) filling out the top five countries by articles published. U.S.-affiliated articles reported on race or ethnicity far more frequently than articles from other countries (Table 3, Fig. 4).

Across all articles, 196 (33.0%) reported a variable that reflected SES. Specific usage (i.e., about reporting education, income, or insurance) ranged widely, as did answer options (Table 2). There were notable differences in how many articles reported SES among the journals, ranging from 32 (15.2%) in NEJM to 28 (21.2%) in Lancet, 51 (34.9%) in JAMA, and 85 (80.2%) in AJE (Fig. 2). Geographic differences were less pronounced than with race and ethnicity but still statistically significant (Table 1, Fig. 4): an SES variable was included in 112 (40.4%) of articles with a U.S. corresponding author and 84 (26.5%) of articles without a U.S. corresponding author (χ2 = 12, p < 0.01). One hundred and three (37.6%) articles with U.S. participants vs. 93 (29.1%) of articles with non-U.S. participants reported SES (χ2 = 4.5, p = 0.03). Almost all AJE authors who reported race or ethnicity also reported an SES variable (55; 85.9%). This was not the case in JAMA (39; 47.0%), NEJM (19; 17.7%), or Lancet (9; 15.5%).

## Discussion

Our results show that race, ethnicity, and SES variables continue to be reported at low rates, and that these variables, along with sex and gender, are often used indistinctly or without clear definition. Moreover, we saw wide variations in these practices by researcher and participant geography, which suggests that cultural or socio-political considerations influence how these variables are used. These results complement and expand on recent findings that the reporting of race, SES, and sex remained limited in the medical literature and had not statistically changed between 2015 and 2019.12,13

Reporting practices for race and ethnicity varied widely, with roughly half of the articles reporting some measure, a finding that aligns with other recent research on this topic.12,13 When researchers do report race or ethnicity, our results suggest that there is little consensus about best practices. Many articles, especially from the U.S., rely on simplistic distinctions (e.g., Black or white, Hispanic or not), as seen in Fig. 3 and Table 2. Even though U.S. agencies request the use of OMB race and ethnicity categories, very few papers actually did this. Even those categories do not meaningfully reflect human diversity, whether genetics, ancestry, experiences of racism, or any other relevant factor. Researchers face a difficult irony: they are often stuck using categories created by racism to study the effects of racism. Meanwhile, many studies rely on single, simple measures of SES (e.g., a three-tiered variable of education or income). These practices do not capture the cumulative impact of social and environmental exposures over a lifetime, especially given the intersecting effects of racism, poverty, and other social determinants.6,24, 25, 26, 27,29

The findings also differed dramatically by author and participant geography. Three-quarters of studies with a U.S. corresponding author or U.S. research participants reported on race or ethnicity, while under one-third of articles published by non-U.S. authors did. The corresponding authors in our sample reported institutional affiliations in thirty-five unique countries. Although the low numbers of articles from many countries complicates nuanced assessments, articles with U.S. corresponding authors by far reported race or ethnicity at higher rates than other countries. SES data were used at similarly low rates across countries. These gaps could reflect different national guidelines for scientific research (e.g., different guidelines provided by funders or journals about the inclusion of diverse populations, or different standards for how such data should be reported). It would be valuable to conduct further research to analyse the history, content, and scientific justifications of these practices. The ubiquity of race in the U.S. medical literature might also reflect distinct political and social values of U.S. researchers and funders. This merits further investigation as well. Importantly, most studies had no explanation of how data on race or ethnicity was collected, whether by patient self-report, chart review, or provider judgement. This widespread omission also impacts the inter-reliability of using these variables.

Socioeconomic status was not widespread in our sample of the medical literature, a finding consistent with that of other recent research on this topic.12,13 Fewer than one-third of articles reported even a single SES variable. SES reporting also differed significantly by geography, though less dramatically than race or ethnicity. It also varied widely between journals, appearing two- to five-times as often in an epidemiology journal (i.e., AJE) compared to the medical journals. In our sample, SES was reported at a rate of 22.7% across NEJM, JAMA, and The Lancet, which was higher than Alegria et al. (2021) reported in those same journals in 2019 (12.3%). This may reflect our broader sample (e.g., not limited to RCTs) or change over a short time, but overall both analyses found that only a small fraction of published articles reported SES.12

The gap between medicine and epidemiology may relate to the histories of these disciplines: when they diverged in the early twentieth century, clinicians focused on individual patients and their cellular pathophysiology while epidemiologists focused on the social and environmental contexts of illness.30 The fields, however, have since converged, with clinicians showing greater interest in the social determinants of health and epidemiologists studying genetics and molecular biology. Our findings reinforce that most medical researchers, however, have not yet brought SES into their research studies. The epidemiology literature shows that it is possible to do so consistently.

Specifying the age of research participants was nearly ubiquitous in our sample. This is unsurprising: age affects disease risk and treatment outcome. It is certainly important to know whether a study was done in children, young adults, or older adults, and that the age distribution in intervention vs. control groups was equivalent. But is age so much more important than all the other variables that it should be reported more often than the others? How often does knowledge of participants’ age (often reported to three significant digits) influence the interpretation of results? Further research could discern whether the universal reporting of age with such exactness is warranted.

Specifying the mix of males and females is almost as common. However, the majority of articles fail to distinguish between biological sex and gender identity. Very few articles acknowledge patients who fall outside the binary, even though trans and nonbinary patients’ inclusion in studies both potentially impacts their care and acknowledges the validity of their identities. Reliance on a male-female distinction reflects assumptions about which aspects of human diversity (e.g., anatomy or karyotype) matter most. Future studies could more concretely identify the best ways to report on the complexity of human sexual orientation and gender identity—characteristics that also shape disease risk and treatment outcomes.

Researchers have to make complex decisions in their quest to transform human experience into data. They face an admittedly difficult task. They have been asked to take seriously certain aspects of human diversity, but consensus about best practices has constantly been in flux. Further complicating matters, choices for language about race, gender, and identity have become politically charged, and the dynamics of all of this differ in each country. While we acknowledge this challenge, we do believe that researchers could do more than most have been doing: after all, a few of the articles in our sample did exhibit considerable sophistication in their demographic reporting as evidenced in Table 2.

Researchers’ decisions have consequences that extend beyond the reported data. For instance, the frequent inclusion of simplistic markers of race (e.g., merely Black or white) reinforces the notion that these “races” are real in a biological sense, a notion with many harmful effects.3,5,30 Any effort invested in finding better ways to measure and write about human diversity (whether race, ethnicity, sex, gender, or age) should include efforts to characterise and report relevant social determinants.10,24,27,31 Only by doing this will we be able to generate the evidence base required for the precision medicine that so many researchers imagine today. Some researchers do manage to use sophisticated markers, and such practices should be within reach of many more.

Many policy interventions could improve how patient demographics are reported. In 2021, editors of several journals issued new guidelines outlining the responsibilities that researchers have to report gender, ethnicity, and SES as often as they do age, sex, or race.32, 33, 34 Surveys of researchers could probe their decisions about what characteristics to include and why they believe those will be meaningful for the interpretation and application of their findings. Research and clinical registration systems could encode variables on, e.g., race and ethnicity with more precision and specificity than the Black-white or Hispanic-not Hispanic dichotomies in order to capture aspects of identity that are distinct from genetic ancestry.35 This new framework could measure directly the things that race and ethnicity are assumed to represent (e.g., experiences of discrimination; diet or other cultural attributes).

Researchers in a variety of fields have developed increasingly sophisticated tools to infer aspects of SES exposure from other demographic data (e.g., address), such as the Harvard Public Health Disparities Geocoding Project, the Area Deprivation Index from the University of Wisconsin, or the U.K Multiple Deprivation Index. Funding agencies such as the NIH or similar agencies in other countries could issue new guidelines for operationalizing demographic characteristics and enforce them through the grant review process.

Limitations of this study include the small dataset of articles from four journals (three medical and one epidemiological) collected from a single year. This was done to allow a detailed, thorough analysis of each article. Larger studies could be done (more journals, more years) but this would require either massive effort or less nuanced analyses. In addition, the small number of articles from many countries limits the conclusions that can be drawn at the country level.

This study generates many possibilities for follow-up research. Analysing the articles by study design (e.g., randomised clinical trial or observational study), by intervention type, by disease, or by specialty discipline may reveal important variations that could be examined by follow-up studies. Adding comparisons across time and with additional journals could help benchmark progress in this area. Qualitative research could be done to interview researchers and discern the extent to which they control or choose the variables they use in the context of the desires or guidelines of funders, journals, or national regulation, or how their existing data are set up.

Clinicians and researchers need to think critically about their use of sex, gender, race, ethnicity, and SES; to justify their decisions; and to report results in a way that is clear and meaningful.7,36 This is not a call to discard concepts like race, ethnicity, or sex, but to handle them—and other important characteristics—with greater sophistication and consistency. We need to be more intentional about when and how we examine, interpret, and report human diversity. Honouring that goal will help us to ask better questions to understand disease risk and treatment outcomes in ways that will benefit all people.
